strengths: Systematic and broad empirical study: the paper evaluates a large set of models (ImageNet-pretrained ResNets/ViTs, DINOv2/v3, OpenPhenom, H-Optimus, UNI/Virchow/GigaPath family) with untrained counterparts, layer-wise probing, and multiple seeds/folds, which gives the central findings reasonable statistical support (e.g., Tables 10-11, Fig. 2).

The diagnostic baselines are well designed and genuinely informative: pixel statistics, untrained encoders, and especially the structure-only cell-graph/point-cloud representations of histology (Section 3.1, Appendix B/D) are a novel and interpretable way to disentangle tissue organization from morphology, supported by a carefully constructed synthetic control dataset (Appendix D.3, Tables 4-5).

The core finding that untrained ViTs and even a SingleConv baseline are competitive with pretrained/foundation models on RxRx3-core gene-gene retrieval, and that pretrained/untrained ViTs produce highly correlated gene-gene rankings (Fig. 1b), is a valuable and actionable negative result for the bioimaging community, mirroring analogous findings in transcriptomics.

The discussion is unusually careful and honest: the authors acknowledge that in-domain models (OpenPhenom, H-Optimus-1, private MAE-G/8) do show clear gains on JUMP-CP and HEST-1k subsets, that the structure-only signal may be partly explained by cell count (Section 5.3, Appendix E.3), and that private backbones limit conclusions (Section 4.1).

Reproducibility is addressed: all datasets are public, evaluation protocols follow published pipelines (HEST, Sanchez et al., Kraus et al.), model configurations are fully specified (Appendix C), and detailed per-dataset results are reported.
weaknesses: Limited methodological originality: the main ideas (untrained/random-network baselines, shortcut detection via simple baselines, PCA dimensionality diagnostics) are adapted from prior work (Zhong & Andreas 2024; transcriptomics benchmark studies), and the contribution is largely a careful transfer of this evaluation methodology to microscopy rather than a new technique or a fundamentally new insight.

The headline claim in the abstract ('state-of-the-art methods perform comparably to these baselines') is overgeneralized relative to the evidence: on JUMP-CP pretrained/foundation models 'consistently outperform' baselines (Section 4.1) and on HEST-1k in-domain models clearly lead (Table 1); the parity result really holds mainly for RxRx3-core, and even there private MAE-G/8 models reach 1.5x higher recall, partially undercutting the pessimistic framing.

The tissue-level analysis relies on a custom coarsened benchmark (HEST-1k-1NN) whose construction (target smoothing over binned spots, larger overlapping patches) plausibly favors structure baselines; although a comparison is provided (Appendix E), the confound is not fully resolved and conclusions are drawn mostly from only four tissue subsets and 50 genes per subset.

Evaluation scope is narrow in places: gene-gene retrieval uses only five literature datasets with recall restricted to the top 5% similarity tail, a cutoff chosen by the authors, and robustness of conclusions to these choices is not systematically examined.

Presentation has notable rough edges: dense small-font figures (Fig. 1a, 3), typos and inconsistencies (e.g., 'Unrained' in Fig. 2, SKCM/SCKM inconsistency between Table 2 and text, stray character in Fig. 6 caption, 'yes, iid'/'yes, ood' formatting in Table 1), and important details deferred to appendices.

Some analyses are suggestive rather than conclusive: the layer-depth trends, dimensionality-performance relationship (Fig. 16), and the claim that pretrained and untrained ViTs 'exploit the same relational signal' rest on correlation-style evidence without intervention experiments; the paper itself concedes that shortcut usage 'invites further interpretability work' (Section 6).

strengths: Broad and careful empirical survey: the paper evaluates a large and current set of foundation models (OpenPhenom, MAE-L/G, H-Optimus-0/1, UNI/UNIv2, Virchow, CONCH, GigaPath, DINOv2/v3) across two biological scales (Cell Painting, histology/spatial transcriptomics) under a consistent frozen-embedding pipeline.

The two proposed diagnostics — untrained encoders and disentangled structure-only cell-graph/point-cloud representations — are sensible, cheap, and genuinely informative; the finding that untrained ViTs and a SingleConv baseline are competitive on RxRx3-core gene-gene retrieval, and that pretrained/untrained ViT rankings are highly correlated (Spearman, Fig. 1b/21), is a concrete and useful observation.
Layer-wise analysis contrasting natural-image depth trends with biological retrieval (Fig. 2, 15) and the dimensionality/collapse diagnostic (Fig. 16) add interpretive value beyond raw rankings.

Generally honest limitation discussion: the paper explicitly flags that structure-only performance may be driven by cell count (Sec. 5.3), that proprietary MAE backbones restrict conclusions (Sec. 4.1), and that strong evidence for arrangement-vs-count would require controlled interventions.

The HEST-1k-1NN coarsening (Appendix B.3, E.1) is a thoughtful instrument for probing whether tissue-scale structure rather than cellular morphology explains performance, and results are reported with fold-wise variance and multiple seeds/initializations (Tables 10-11).
weaknesses: The central thesis — that strong simple baselines rival foundation models and that benchmark metrics mask shortcuts — is already well established for transcriptomics (Luecken et al., 2022; Bendidi et al., 2024; Ahlmann-Eltze et al., 2025; Csendes et al., 2025), which the paper itself acknowledges. The transfer of this argument to microscopy is the main novelty, but the paper does not sharply articulate what is conceptually new beyond repeating the protocol in a second modality.

The headline claim rests on heavily subsampled, custom variants of the benchmarks: RxRx3-core is reduced to 10 images per gene over three folds, JUMP-CP uses only eight positive-control compounds, and HEST-1k-1NN is a self-introduced coarsening. It is unclear whether 'untrained ViTs match pretrained models' reflects a genuine property of the learned representations or an artifact of the reduced evaluation, and the paper does not test this on the full protocols.

The most striking positive result — MAE-L/8 and MAE-G/8 in-domain embeddings reaching 1.5x higher recall than all pretrained and untrained baselines (Sec. 4.1, Appendix H) — substantially undercuts the abstract's claim that 'state-of-the-art methods perform comparably to these baselines' and 'existing models fail to consistently acquire high-level, biologically meaningful features.' The abstract and Sec. 5.1 do not adequately reconcile this contradiction.

The structure-only analysis is not conditioned on the acknowledged cell-count confound; the paper admits that a matched or count-controlled analysis on real tissue is missing, leaving the most interesting tissue-level claim (Sec. 5.3) speculative. Small sample sizes compound this (e.g., HEST subsets with 2-4 slides and 2 patients in Table 2), making fold-averaged PCC differences difficult to interpret.

No code or artifact release is mentioned, which is a significant reproducibility gap for a benchmarking paper whose main contribution is an evaluation protocol (custom RxRx3-core subsampling, JUMP-CP subset construction, HEST-1k-1NN, channel-expansion schemes, hand-crafted cell-count features).

Presentation is not at the level expected for the main track: numerous typos and grammatical errors ('Unrained' in Fig. 2, 'We used these shared controls are used' in B.2, SCKM vs SKCM inconsistency across Tables 2/8, 'pretained', 'concordation'), some main-text figures (Figs. 1-3) are effectively unreadable at native resolution and require the upscaled Appendix I versions, and the main-text results section relies heavily on appendix material.

No significance testing or effect-size analysis supports the many 'competitive'/'comparable' claims; several conclusions (e.g., COAD structure-vs-image competitiveness in Table 1, where structure 0.31 vs OOD image 0.30) rest on differences well within reported standard deviations.

The synthetic-data study (Appendix D.3) is interesting but weakly connected: none of the models reach perfect scores, and the paper's own conclusion ('opens a promising direction') does not validate any substantive claim used in the main results.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely question: whether microscopy foundation models learn biologically meaningful high-level features or merely exploit dataset shortcuts, and does so with a systematic, benchmark-focused study spanning two key scales (cell culture via RxRx3-core and JUMP-CP; tissue via HEST-1k and a new HEST-1k-1NN variant).

The proposed baseline families (pixel statistics, untrained/random encoders, disentangled tissue-structure representations) are simple, well-motivated, and genuinely diagnostic; the untrained-model comparison and Spearman analysis of gene-gene rankings (Fig. 1b) provide direct, interpretable evidence that pretrained and untrained ViTs exploit largely the same relational signal on RxRx3-core.

Careful and thorough experimental hygiene: multiple random seeds and folds (Tables 10-11), intermediate-layer probing to contrast ImageNet vs. microscopy behavior (Fig. 2), representational-dimensionality diagnostics (Fig. 16), and controlled synthetic graph experiments (Appendix D.3) that separate cell count from spatial arrangement.

Honest treatment of limitations, including the confound between structure-only performance and cell count (Sec. 5.3, E.3), the caveat that proprietary MAE backbones limit conclusions about high-level abstraction (Sec. 4.1), and the admission that structure-only gains do not yet prove arrangement (rather than count) drives performance.

The mixed-but-nuanced findings (in-domain pretraining clearly helps on HEST subsets and some JUMP-CP compounds; structure-only models surprisingly competitive on PRAD/COAD) are presented conservatively and give the community actionable guidance for interpreting benchmark scores.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the core message — that simple baselines can rival foundation models and that benchmark scores can be inflated by confounders — was already established for transcriptomics (Luecken et al. 2022, Bendidi et al. 2024, Ahlmann-Eltze et al. 2025, etc.), and untrained-network phenomena are well documented (Ulyanov et al., Zhong & Andreas). The contribution is largely a transfer of known diagnostic methodology to a new modality rather than a new insight.

A tension between the abstract's headline claim ('state-of-the-art methods perform comparably to these baselines') and the actual results, which are mixed: on JUMP-CP and HEST-1k in-domain models consistently and substantially outperform baselines. The framing risks overstating the negative result, and the discussion (Sec. 5.1) walks this back.

Several key benchmarks are author-modified subsets (subsampled three-fold RxRx3-core with 10 images per gene, custom JUMP-CP subset of positive controls only, newly constructed HEST-1k-1NN). This complicates direct comparability with prior published results, and some conclusions (e.g., structure-only competitiveness) may be sensitive to these construction choices even though the HEST-1k vs. HEST-1k-1NN alignment analysis partially mitigates this concern.

Reproducibility is not clearly established: no explicit code/artifact release statement appears in the manuscript, and reproducing the pipeline requires combining many external assets (CellViT segmentations, HEST protocol, custom folds, channel-adaptation schemes described only in Appendix C.4).

Presentation issues in the main text: several central figures (Fig. 1a, Fig. 3, Fig. 17-20) are dense and hard to read at print size, forcing reliance on upscaled appendix versions; the 'Meaningfulness Statement' is unusual and philosophical, and the paper would benefit from sharper separation between empirical findings and interpretation.

Statistical support for some contrasts is thin: e.g., claims about layer-wise trends and per-compound analyses rest on small numbers of folds/seeds, and the observation that untrained models outperform trained ResNets on retrieval is reported but not fully explained mechanistically.

strengths: Systematic and broad empirical study spanning both organizational scales (Cell Painting / cell culture via RxRx3-core, JUMP-CP, JUMP-MoA; tissue via HEST-1k, HEST-1k-1NN, BRACS, BACH), with many model families (ResNets, ViTs, DINOv2/v3, OpenPhenom, H-Optimus, GigaPath, Virchow, etc.), multiple seeds and folds, which lends credibility to the headline finding that untrained ViTs, pixel statistics, and a minimal SingleConv baseline are competitive with pretrained/foundation models on RxRx3-core gene retrieval.

The proposed calibration baselines are well motivated and conceptually clean: untrained encoders separate architectural inductive bias from learned biology, pixel statistics probe low-level signal, and structure-only cell-graph/point-cloud representations isolate tissue organization from morphology. The layer-wise analysis and PCA dimensionality diagnostic, contrasted against ImageNet-1k kNN probing, provide genuinely informative interpretive tools (e.g., pretrained and untrained ViTs yield highly correlated gene-gene rankings, Spearman ~0.8).

Careful protocol engineering: multi-fold variance estimation, restriction to the informative top-5% tail of RxRx3-core with justification (Fig. 23), synthetic Poisson-process graph datasets to validate what GNN/vision encoders can extract beyond cell count, and explicit cell-count control analyses (Fig. 17, Table 7).
Strong reproducibility posture: all data and models are public or released as embeddings, code is released, and evaluation protocols are documented in detail (Appendices A–B).

Honest limitations discussion: the authors acknowledge that cell count may drive much of the structure-only performance, that proprietary MAE backbones prevent layer-wise analysis, and that their conclusions rest on prediction alignment rather than mechanistic interpretability. Table 1/Table 8 results are presented with per-fold deviations, and the in-domain vs. OOD split is informative.
weaknesses: The central claim — that benchmark scores 'mask a lack of relevant high-level abstractions' — is stronger than the evidence supports. All conclusions are drawn from frozen-embedding linear/kNN/regression probing; the alternative explanation that retrieval tasks have an inherent low ceiling or weak label-alignment (rather than models lacking abstractions) is not conclusively ruled out, and fine-tuning results are absent. The scope of 'what models really learn' should be tempered to 'what frozen embeddings certify under these metrics'.

Several core findings replicate known results rather than break new ground: the competitive strength of untrained/random-feature baselines follows Zhong & Andreas (2024) and the transcriptomics literature the authors themselves cite (Bendidi, Ahlmann-Eltze, Seal), and batch-effect/shortcut concerns in microscopy benchmarks (RxRx1, Arevalo et al.) are already well documented. The originality lies mainly in the systematic transfer of this calibration methodology to microscopy, which is useful but incremental.

The structure-only tissue contribution is partially undermined by the authors' own analysis: cell-count baselines are strong, gene-wise PCC of graph models correlates strongly with cell count (Fig. 17), and synthetic-data pretraining of GNNs yields inconsistent gains (Table 2, e.g., negative deltas for EGNN). Section 5.4 correctly flags this as an open causal question, so the positive framing of 'spatial organization is a strong modality' remains speculative.

The tissue-level evidence base is thin: several HEST-1k subsets use only 2 patients (Table 3), making patient-stratified cross-validation folds and the claim that 'structure-based models are competitive with OOD encoders on PRAD/COAD' statistically fragile; no significance testing is reported for these comparisons.

The modified RxRx3-core protocol (top-5% tail only, three folds, 10 images/gene subsample) deviates from the original benchmark; the comparison to original scores exists (Fig. 18) but the re-calibrated numbers complicate direct comparability with prior published rankings.

Presentation has notable rough edges: a few grammatical errors ('It is generally generally true', 'human brest tissue'), figures with dense/ambiguous legends (Fig. 2, Fig. 5), and key quantitative claims (e.g., '1.5 times higher recall' for MAE-G/8) deferred entirely to appendices. Some interpretive claims about depth (Fig. 4) average heterogeneous architectures, which risks masking model-specific behavior.

strengths: The study is unusually broad and systematic: it evaluates a large set of backbones (ResNets, ViTs, DINOv2/v3, OpenPhenom, H-Optimus-1, GNNs) across cell culture (RxRx3-core, JUMP-CP, JUMP-MoA/SPACe), tissue (HEST-1k and a newly proposed binned HEST-1k-1NN variant), and natural images (ImageNet-1k reference), with multiple folds and seeds, which is appropriate for a benchmark-critique paper.

The core methodological idea — using deliberately 'uninformed' baselines (pixel statistics, randomly initialized encoders, SingleConv) to calibrate what a benchmark score certifies — is sound and well-motivated by the analogous findings in transcriptomics (Luecken, Bendidi, Ahlmann-Eltze, Csendes), and the paper positions itself carefully relative to that literature.

The disentangled tissue-structure baseline (cell-centroid graphs/point clouds from CellViT segmentations) is a genuinely interesting diagnostic, and the synthetic-graph experiments (Appendix C.3) are a thoughtful attempt to control for cell count and test whether encoders recover organization beyond density.

Layer-wise analysis is a useful addition: the observation that performance decreases or saturates with depth on biological retrieval while increasing on ImageNet (Fig. 4), and that in-domain models (H-Optimus-1, OpenPhenom) improve with depth while OOD/untrained models do not (Fig. 26), is a concrete, actionable diagnostic.

The discussion is appropriately cautious in places (e.g., Sec. 5.4 explicitly flags the cell-count confound for structure-only results and notes that 'stronger evidence would require matching analysis'), and Sec. 5.1 advocates a 'conservative reading' of absolute scores rather than overclaiming. Code is released and most data/models are public.

Several concrete findings are valuable to practitioners: the near-random retrieval for some JUMP-CP positive controls across all models, the weak bottom-5% tail in RxRx3-core (Fig. 23), and the CellProfiler-vs-untrained-ViT alignment (Table 13).
weaknesses: The headline claim — that 'existing models fail to consistently acquire high-level, biologically meaningful features' — is stronger than the evidence supports. Results are heterogeneous: on JUMP-CP 'pretrained and foundation models consistently outperform untrained and pixel-based baselines'; on HEST-1k, in-domain pretraining offers 'a clear advantage' on CCRCC/COAD/SKCM and H-Optimus-1 improves with depth; and MAE-G/8 reaches 1.5x the best baselines on RxRx3-core. The 'surprising' result is essentially confined to RxRx3-core recall@5% (where all models score ~0.16–0.20 vs. a 0.05 random baseline, i.e., all are weak), yet the abstract and title generalize it across bioimaging.

Limited novelty of the central observation. That untrained ViTs and simple baselines can match trained models on certain tasks is already established (Zhong & Andreas 2024; Baek et al. 2021; deep image prior line; cell-count benchmarks in Seal et al. 2025), and the 'simple baselines rival foundation models' narrative is explicitly imported from transcriptomics. The paper's incremental contribution is applying these diagnostics to microscopy benchmarks, which weakens its significance for the main track.

The structure-only tissue finding — arguably the paper's most original component — is undermined by the authors' own analysis: Fig. 17 and Appendix D.3 show strong correlation between structure-only performance and a cell-count baseline, and Sec. 5.4 concedes that 'it does not yet prove that arrangement (rather than count) drives the gains.' The EGNN synthetic-pretraining results are inconsistent (Table 2), leaving the mechanistic story unresolved.

The RxRx3-core evaluation deviates from the official benchmark protocol (restricting to the top 5% similarity tail, three subsampled folds with 10 images/gene). While motivated by the uninformative lower tail (Fig. 23), this changes the task definition, and cross-checks against original scores (Fig. 18) appear only in the appendix; a stronger justification of protocol equivalence is needed to rule out that conclusions are protocol artifacts.

Some interpretive analyses are correlational rather than causal: the PCA-explained-variance / recall relationship (Fig. 20, 25) conflates architecture family (ResNet vs. ViT) with dimensionality, and the paper itself admits that 'effective dimensionality is therefore a useful sanity check... but it does not establish biological semantics.' The Spearman-ranking correlations between pretrained and untrained ViTs are suggestive but the underlying shared signal is never identified.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track paper: multiple typos and errors ('Unrained' in Fig. 4 legend, 'Fondation Model' in Table 13, 'brest tissue,' 'generally generally true,' 'We used these shared controls are used,' an incomplete sentence in Sec. 3.2, the mAP axis in Fig. 26 labeled 'ImageNet Retrieval' for JUMP-CP), several figures with tiny, hard-to-read legends (Figs. 5, 18, 22), and an incomplete/garbled reference (Groger et al. 2026, 'aristotelian biew').

Missing related analyses that would strengthen the causal story: no intervention experiments (e.g., permuting spatial coordinates or matching on cell count on real tissue) are performed despite being identified as 'stronger evidence' in Sec. 5.4; the limitation that only public foundation models can be studied layer-wise (with the best RxRx3 model, MAE-G/8, remaining proprietary) further narrows the scope of the conclusions.

strengths: Comprehensive, well-executed empirical study spanning both organizational scales (cell culture: RxRx3-core, JUMP-CP, JUMP-MoA; tissue: HEST-1k, HEST-1k-1NN, BRACS, BACH) with a large, relevant set of pretrained and untrained encoders (ResNets, ViTs, DINOv2/v3, OpenPhenom, H-Optimus-1, many pathology foundation models), all under consistent evaluation pipelines.

The untrained-encoder and pixel-statistics baselines provide a genuinely useful calibration tool: the finding that untrained ViTs and even a SingleConv baseline are competitive with pretrained/foundation models on RxRx3-core gene–gene retrieval (with correlated gene-gene rankings, Fig. 3/24) is a striking and actionable result, supported by stability checks (3 seeds, 3 folds) and a hyperparameter sweep (Table 10).

The structure-only tissue representation (nuclei-centroid graphs/point clouds) is a clever ablation that exposes how much of HEST-1k signal is explainable by spatial organization alone, including the honest follow-up analysis showing a large part of the effect may reduce to cell count (Fig. 17, Appendix D.3).

The ImageNet-1k reference and the layer-wise analysis (Figs. 4, 7) are valuable diagnostics showing that depth behaves differently in microscopy vs. natural images, and the effective-dimensionality analysis gives a testable correlate of representational collapse.

Good research hygiene: metric modifications to RxRx3-core (top-tail restriction, multi-fold variance) are justified and documented; code is released, all data/models public; limitations are candidly discussed (e.g., private MAE-G/8 backbones limiting conclusions, the unresolved cell-count confound in Sec. 5.4).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the paper's core devices (untrained/random encoders, simple statistical baselines, spatial cell-organization features) are all established, and the paper itself situates the contribution as transplanting a lesson already demonstrated in transcriptomics (Luecken et al., Bendidi et al., Seal et al., etc.). The contribution is diagnostic rather than methodological, which narrows its reach.

The central negative claim ('benchmarks fail to certify high-level abstractions') is supported mainly by performance parity and ranking correlation; the authors acknowledge (Sec. 6) that demonstrating models actually exploit shortcuts would require interpretability work that is not provided, so the causal interpretation remains plausible but not established.

The cell-count confound for structure-only models is acknowledged but not resolved on real tissue (Sec. 5.4); synthetic experiments (C.3) show encoders can go beyond count, but the paper concedes that 'explicitly demonstrating their utility... is difficult to achieve' — so the headline tissue-level result (structure-only ≈ H-Optimus-1 on PRAD/COAD) is weakened.

Benchmark coverage has gaps: comparisons across the strongest cell-culture models are constrained because the best in-domain MAE-G/8 backbone is private and only available for one dataset via precomputed embeddings; some subtyping results are secondary to GrapHist rather than a full independent evaluation.

Presentation is uneven: numerous typographical and grammatical errors ('generally generally', 'brest tissue', 'Unrained', 'Fondation Model', 'concordation'), awkward phrasing ('we focus only on a subset of data. Namely, ...'), and inconsistent capitalization of 'iid/IID' in Table 1; some figure content (e.g., Fig. 22b) is difficult to parse.

Multiple probes (compound-specific, gene-specific, per-dataset) increase the risk of selective interpretation of subset-level effects; while error bars and folds are reported, statistical tests distinguishing 'comparable' from 'not clearly different' are largely absent.
